replies.body: Found a money bug in practice options: an expired trade (every Close Call practice trade) settled at whatever the stock was worth when you next opened Portfolio, not at the expiration-day close. On expiration morning it settled at the 10am price; a week later, at that week's price. So a Close Call YES that was right at Friday's close could show as a total loss on Monday. Now it settles at the official close on expiration day; until that close is in, Portfolio shows the trade as 'Settling' with an estimate, and it can't be closed by hand at an after-hours price.

A practice gain on its own says little: +$300 when the market rose 5% on the same money is worse than buying the index, and a finance professor judges every portfolio against a benchmark. Portfolio now has a 'You vs the S&P 500' card (your trades +$X, same money in the S&P 500 +$Y, ahead/behind by $Z, N of M beat the index) and each trade shows its own S&P line. Measured close to close in New York time, no look-ahead; the card says how.

Selling a practice position used to make it vanish: Portfolio said 'Nothing here yet' and the gain was only buried in Account value. Portfolio now has a Closed trades list: each sale or closed/expired options trade with what it cost, what came back and the gain, plus 'Locked in: +$X on N trades'. The gains add up to the account's total.

A finance professor would catch a 'Paramount' media call graded on a $3 penny stock (PARA's ticker now belongs to Parabolic Technologies), and it scored a fake 70-point win. The app now checks that each ticker is the company the idea names and drops it if not: about 25 of 1,439 real pairs were the wrong company (Philip Morris -> Picard Medical, BYD -> Boyd Gaming).

The brain learns each news headline and its opposite. Some opposites still bet the same way as the headline on a different stock (the opposite of 'Bitcoin's selloff may signal a longer crypto downturn' was learned as QQQ down). Now an opposite whose bets all go the headline's way is dropped; opposites with real winners and losers (publishers down, META up) are kept.

A finance professor would flag 'Market regime: Calm, markets are quiet' with the S&P 500 at 22% volatility and 3% off its high. 'Calm' really meant 'anything that isn't a steady climb or turbulent', so it now says 'In between' and shows the three numbers and the rule.

Close Call showed 'NVDA above $150' odds taken from the $149/$152.5 spread, which is really the chance of a close above $150.75 (1-2 pts off). The odds are now read at $150 itself from the strikes either side, and the note under them says which prices were used.

Close Call showed AAPL at 50% odds to close above $360 while YES cost $204 for a $500 payout (41%): a finance professor would call that a free-money bug. Each strike is now priced at its own implied volatility, so YES costs the market's own spread price and agrees with the odds.

A user who saw '+9 pts' on a call had no way to tell skill from luck. My beliefs now marks each graded call on the spread of calls like it (e.g. 'in the best 1 in 10; about 1 in 10 calls do this well, so one call still says little about skill').

The brain learns each news headline and its opposite. 4 in 10 opposites were bet the same way as the headline (e.g. 'I don't think the retail recovery will stall' -> Target down). Now a stock can't be bet the same way on both sides, and users who type 'I don't think...' get the opposite bet.
